note: Cheap power and TVA in the north, Alabama Power elsewhere; receptive utilities. Hot, humid climate and tornado exposure. First local moratoriums (Anniston, Westover) adopted Aug 2026.
Free cooling and water, but an isolated grid, very high power prices, seismic risk and almost no fiber ecosystem.

Phoenix is a top-tier market with roughly 100 operating sites, but the 2026 budget (SB 1861, signed June 13) bars new data center sales tax exemption applications from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2029; 113 applications rushed in during the last two weeks. The Colorado River Tier 1 shortage, in place since 2022, trims Arizona's supply about 18% again in 2026. Backlash is now regulatory: Tucson adopted data center rules Aug 5, Pima County imposed a 120-day moratorium Aug 11, and Pinal County denied the La Osa rezoning Aug 26, 2026.

srcs.t: Sonoran Desert data centers update, Aug 2026

note: Low industrial rates, Entergy Arkansas has courted large loads, little organized opposition so far. Limited fiber depth and tornado exposure.

Unmatched connectivity but the highest industrial power price in the lower 48, transformer shortages leaving built facilities unpowered, and the first voter-approved citywide ban (Monterey Park, June 2026) plus a Coachella Valley restriction bloc. Seismic and wildfire risk.
Denver is a solid secondary market with cool, dry air. Xcel capacity is tight, Colorado River basin water stress is severe, and hail and wildfire losses are high.
ISO-NE power is scarce and expensive; Groton enacted a local moratorium. Low natural hazard exposure is the main upside.
PJM capacity pricing at the cap flows into Delmarva bills; Dover is weighing an 18-month pause and Harrington rejected a data center ordinance in Aug 2026.

Miami is a key interconnection hub for Latin America and FPL is building generation, but the 2026 Hyperscale Data Center Act raised the exemption threshold to 100 MW and at least eight counties adopted one-year moratoriums in mid-2026. Hurricane exposure is the worst in the country.

Atlanta is a top-tier growth market. Georgia PSC approved 9,885 MW of new Georgia Power generation in Dec 2025 mostly for large loads; the large-load pipeline reached ~69 GW. The sales tax exemption survived a repeal push and runs through 2032, but 28 local moratoriums (Savannah, Rockdale, Newton and others) make site entitlement harder.
By far the highest power price in the US and an island grid; not a development target.
Cheap hydro-heavy power, cool dry climate, sales tax exemption on server equipment, Meta's Kuna campus as anchor. Record-low 2026 snowpack is a water flag; fiber ecosystem is thin.

Chicago is a top-five market, but ComEd's large-load queue holds 28 GW of requests against a 24 GW all-time peak, PJM's 2028/29 capacity auction cleared at the price cap, and Gov. Pritzker directed DCEO to stop signing new Data Center Investment Program agreements from July 1, 2026, with no end date set (his budget proposal framed it as two years). Great Lakes water is a strength.

srcs.t: Capitol News Illinois on ComEd large-load pipeline

note: The most incentive-friendly large state: 50-year exemptions, an estimated $8.2B package to Amazon, and AEP/Duke territories delivering capacity faster than eastern PJM. Elkhart stopped accepting applications until Dec 2027, and HB 1333 would route revenue to host towns.

Abundant wind, MidAmerican has been receptive to large loads, established hyperscale presence (Microsoft, Meta, Google) around Des Moines. Woodbury County adopted a 12-month pause. Derecho and tornado exposure.
Evergy has spare capacity and the state offers incentives; Kansas City metro gives some ecosystem. Tornado and hail losses are high and western water is stressed.
Second-cheapest industrial power east of the Mississippi, LG&E/KU and TVA territory, incentives intact. Modest fiber depth; flood and tornado exposure.
Second-cheapest industrial power in the country and Entergy won approval for new gas plants to serve Meta's Hyperion campus. Hurricane and flood exposure and a hot, humid climate are the trade-offs.

The legislature passed the first statewide moratorium (LD 307); Gov. Mills vetoed it April 24, 2026 and the override failed, but LD 713 stripped incentive eligibility and the Jay mill project was halted in June. Bangor and Eastport have local bans.
Frederick County spillover from Northern Virginia, but PJM constraints, above-average power prices, a Baltimore moratorium and a proposed statewide pause (HB 120).
Expensive ISO-NE power with little headroom; no state incentive program. Cool climate and low hazard exposure.

Gov. Whitmer is the most pro-investment governor of the cycle (OpenAI Stargate 'The Barn' in Saline), with a 2024 exemption and a July 2026 Responsible Growth Pledge. But 35 local moratoriums are tracked, and DTE/Consumers generation is still catching up. Great Lakes water and a cold climate are strong.

Cold climate and abundant water; Meta (Rosemount) and Microsoft (Becker) anchor the market. The 2025 law kept the equipment exemption but ended the electricity exemption and added fees; Xcel capacity is the constraint.
Very low power prices, aggressive incentives, AWS's $10B Madison County build and Compass in Meridian. Hot and humid; tornado exposure; thin fiber ecosystem.
Kansas City and St. Louis offer connectivity; incentives available. Peculiar enacted a local ban and Ameren/Evergy headroom is moderate.

CNBC's grid analysis puts Montana among the ten best-positioned states on price and reliability; cold climate helps PUE. The grid is small, fiber is sparse, wildfire and drought are the physical risks.
Public power (OPPD/NPPD) has been receptive; Google, Meta and Microsoft cluster around Omaha. Second-cheapest residential power nationally. Tornado exposure.
Reno and Las Vegas have established campuses and partial tax abatements, but Lake Mead sits at ~32% and Reno's water use is contested. Low seismic and storm losses.
Expensive New England power and no headroom; otherwise a low-risk cold-climate location.

The state froze its $250M AI data center incentive, then enacted the Data Center Fair Share Act (July 7, 2026) creating a separate rate class and requiring data centers to curtail before residents. 72 tracked local moratoriums, the most of any state. Strong NYC-adjacent connectivity.
Cheapest industrial electricity in the US (5.43¢/kWh in 2024) and on CNBC's best-grid list; Meta's Los Lunas campus anchors. Water stress and thin fiber are the limits.

Executive Order 62 (July 14, 2026) holds discretionary DEC permits for data centers of 50 MW or more in abeyance until the Generic Environmental Impact Statement is finished, framed as up to one year; the legislature's broader 20 MW bill (S10642) awaits delivery to the governor and action by Dec 31. ESD's Community Investment Framework proposes $1M per MW as a starting contribution. Excluded: applications deemed complete before July 14, and facilities primarily used for manufacturing, research, education or medical care.

The 2026 budget permanently repealed the sales tax exemption on data center electricity (effective Aug 6, 2026) while keeping equipment exemptions. Charlotte (150-day), Durham County (9-month) and Apex passed moratoriums. Duke Energy headroom is tightening.

srcs.t: EY tax alert on the electricity exemption repeal

note: Cheapest commercial power in the country, abundant gas and wind, receptive utilities, cold climate and low hazard exposure. Applied Digital's Ellendale campus proves scale is possible. Very thin fiber and labor pool.

Columbus is a top emerging market and CNBC ranks Ohio No. 9 for power available to computing (SoftBank's 10 GW Piketon campus broke ground March 2026). But Gov. DeWine paused new exemption approvals after the Tax Credit Authority's June 1, 2026 meeting pending a joint legislative committee study, HB 957 would bar new exemptions from Oct 1, 2026, 35 local moratoriums are tracked and councils have begun rejecting site plans.

srcs.t: Data Center Frontier on SoftBank Piketon
CNBC Best States for AI Data Centers 2026

note: Third-cheapest industrial power and Google's Pryor campus; HB 2992 (effective July 1, 2026) requires large loads to fund their own grid costs. SB 1488 statewide moratorium and HB 4424 property tax rollback were proposed but not enacted; Oklahoma City passed a local pause. Tornado alley.

Hillsboro's cable landings and Prineville/The Dalles campuses are mature, but BPA transmission and PGE capacity are constrained and the 2025 POWER Act shifts costs onto large loads. Cascadia seismic risk; cool climate is ideal for cooling.

Second-highest power supply available for computing per CNBC, nuclear restarts and new gas, and Amazon's $20B commitment. Shapiro's GRID Standards (May 2026) make the sales tax exemption conditional on clean-firm generation, LEED Gold and 50 jobs at 125% of average wage. PJM capacity costs and many township-level fights.
Among the most expensive power in the lower 48 with no headroom.

Exemption covers both equipment and electricity; Palmetto Sites readiness funding jumped to $80M in 2026 with 51 pre-vetted sites. Santee Cooper and Dominion SC have headroom and a VC Summer restart is under study. Hurricane exposure on the coast.
On CNBC's best-grid list, but SB 135 / HB 1038 (2026) add disclosure and cost-allocation rules using a 10 MW threshold, and there is no dedicated incentive. Sparse fiber.
TVA power at 6.21¢/kWh, CNBC's top water availability score, incentives intact, Oak Ridge and Nashville ecosystems, xAI's Memphis campus (with a contested gas turbine fight). Tornado exposure.

The largest pipeline in the country (roughly 1,000 projects under construction or planned) and Dallas is the second-largest market. But Gov. Abbott's Aug 3, 2026 directive paused all pending data center interconnections until each project passes a PUCT/ERCOT audit, due Dec 10; ERCOT was weighing ~474 GW of large-load requests (about 90% data centers) and halted Batch Zero classifications. SB 6 already allows curtailment of 75 MW+ loads. The sales tax exemption survives until at least the 2027 session. Water is strained statewide.

Holland & Knight on the exemption's legislative risk

note: Executive Order 2026-03 (May 29) directs executive-branch agencies to apply a 'higher bar' to large data center review, requiring that water consumption not increase and that Great Salt Lake impacts be weighed, after the 9 GW Stratos proposal in Box Elder County triggered a referendum campaign now in district court. Dry, cool climate and Salt Lake City connectivity remain positives.

srcs.t: Box Elder County, Stratos referendum page
Utah News Dispatch on the referendum appeal

note: Gov. Scott vetoed H.727's restrictions (May 28, 2026) and the override failed, but the grid is tiny and power is expensive. Lowest natural hazard exposure in the country.

Still the world's largest market (Northern Virginia ~13% of global capacity, 0.2% vacancy, all 2026 deliveries pre-committed) but the hardest place to get power: Dominion has quoted 7-year waits for 100 MW since 2024, had ~54 GW under contract by July 2026 and ~70 GW of requests in queue. The 2026 budget left the sales tax exemption in place through 2035 but added a $0.011/kWh electricity consumption tax from July 1, 2026 (collections above $600M/yr refunded, sunsets June 2028), HB 153 requires site assessments before local zoning approvals for 100 MW+ projects, and DEQ must define Cooling Water Scarcity Areas by July 2027.

Budget Item 366 #7c, Cooling Water Scarcity Areas

note: Cheap hydro and a cool climate put Washington atop CNBC's grid ranking; Quincy and Seattle are established markets. Grant County PUD is effectively full and BPA transmission is the bottleneck; the exemption is limited to rural counties; Snohomish County paused applications through Dec 2026.

HB 2014 (2025) created a certified microgrid district program letting data centers self-supply from coal or gas; Berkeley County is a Northern Virginia spillover. Rural opposition (Tucker County) is emerging; fiber is thin.

Microsoft (Mount Pleasant) and Meta (Beaver Dam) anchor a fast-growing market with a 2023 exemption and Great Lakes water. We Energies' gas buildout is contested and Port Washington-style local fights are frequent.

Gov. Gordon's EO 2026-03 ('Data Centers the Wyoming Way', June 3) explicitly keeps the state open for investment while making developers pay for new power; Cheyenne hosts a 1.8 GW Crusoe/Tallgrass campus. Cold, cheap, low-hazard, but very thin fiber and labor.
